Easy ground leads to the tooth's summit. Getting down into the southern notch means either a rappel off tat or a low 5th downclimb. text.approach: From High Bridge, take the Park Creek trail up the Park Creek valley and climb to the snow line on the south side of the saddle between Goode and Storm King; the first party camped there. Gain the saddle, make one rappel onto the glacier on the north side, and descend it through crevasses and beneath an ice cliff to the foot of the roughly 3,000 ft rock rib that leads straight to the main (east) summit. Expect a bivy at the base of the rib.

text.approach: Drive WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Ross Dam Trailhead (MP 134). Descend about 1 mile on the Ross Dam trail/service road to Ross Lake, then cross via the Ross Lake Resort water taxi (on-demand, ~$4-5/person) or by hiking/paddling around, and pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake. Follow it roughly 10 miles to Luna Camp, then continue about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage; leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley (staying on its north side is recommended) to the open basin east of Luna Peak (~4,300 ft) — described as the easiest, least-brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, climb to Access Col, cross to Luna Col, and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss–Fury saddle. An alternate southern approach reaches Swiss via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mt. Crowder's NE ridge down to a camp at Pickell Pass, from which Swiss's south side is climbed directly.

text.overview: Swiss Peak has no independently approached line — it is climbed as a link in Picket Range crest traverses. The most-documented ascent gains the West Fury–Swiss col over a small glacier/snowfield, then climbs unusually solid rock up Swiss's southwest face to the broad NW–SE summit ridge; an alternate class 3 line ascends the south side directly from Pickell Pass, and parties approaching from the north describe an 'easy way up' from the Spectre Plateau.
text.descent: There is no independent 'summit and go home' descent — retreat means reversing whichever approach line was used. From the summit, downclimb near the northwest ridge back toward the saddle with West Fury, re-cross the glacier/snowfield, and either return to a West Fury camp or continue the high traverse. Parties on the southern line downclimb the class 3 south side directly back to the Pickell Pass

Traverse the glacier to the col just west of Tenpeak and the base of the north couloir.

text.overview: A prominent snow/ski couloir splitting Tenpeak's north face, reached by traversing in from the Honeycomb Glacier; a sustained ~35-degree, roughly 1,200-ft snow climb finishes with one short 5.4 rock pitch to the summit via the NW Ridge.
text.descent: From the summit, reverse the short 5.4 pitch back to the top of the couloir. Ski parties descend the couloir itself (firm corn snow in the morning softening through the day); climbers on foot downclimb the ~1,200-ft, up-to-35-degree snow to the Honeycomb Glacier and retrace the approach.

text.descent: From the South Brother summit, descend the South Brother's standard route rather than reversing the ridge traverse: go down the east-facing gully to the 5,500 ft base camp area, then retrace the trail descent to Lena Lake Trailhead (additional 4-5 hours).

text.approach: Via the multi-day Goodell Creek approach to a camp on the Chopping Block ridge (~6,400 ft) or the col separating the peak from the main Picket Range; from there, walk and scramble (some exposed 3rd class) southwest to the base of the ridge.

text.overview: The peak's classic technical route: 4 pitches of alpine rock up the northeast ridge, established by the Firey party in 1970, with a steep 5.5 crux about 100 ft below the summit.
text.descent: Descend by rappelling the ridge itself — most parties use a 70m rope to reach most stations comfortably; one reporting party got down on a 50m rope with a tagline. Existing fixed rap slings have been reported along the route.

text.approach: Via the multi-day Goodell Creek approach to a camp on the Chopping Block ridge (~6,400 ft); the route starts up the lower NE Ridge before diverging onto the north face traverse.

text.overview: A new route rather than the peak's first ascent, climbed in 1961 by Ed Cooper and Glen Denny, ascending to the base of the north ridge, diagonally traversing the northwest face, and topping out via the west ridge. A 2008 party described a similar line as starting up the NE Ridge before an exposed class-4 traverse across the north face gains the NW ridge for an easy class-3 finish.
text.descent: Rather than reverse the exposed class 4 ledges of the north face, rappel the Northeast Ridge on a single rope, using the fixed slings along it, back to the camp on the Chopping Block ridge (about 6,400 ft). The way out from there is long and steep: work across Stump Hollow, a mix of snow, slab and heather, up to the Barrier crest, follow a faint path down the crest from timberline (about 5,600 ft)

text.overview: A short, striking single-pitch 5.4 that climbs bouldery face moves into a deep, well-protected chimney on The Fin's northeast side, then an easy 3rd-class scramble gains the true summit.

text.approach: The drive itself is easy — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek Trailhead, about 23 miles total — but the climb to Cathedral Peak is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state. From the trailhead, the Andrews Creek Trail (#504) climbs roughly 12 miles to 6,680+ ft Andrews Pass, then descends into the Spanish Creek drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lakes below the peak's southwest side, putting the one-way approach at around 18 miles with significant elevation gain and loss along the way. Most parties treat this as a 2-4 day backpack (roughly 40+ miles round trip), camping at or near Cathedral Lakes before making a summit push. A free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead, along with a trailhead parking pass; the first many miles are a hot, rocky, buggy uphill slog with little shade, so this is genuinely a remote, multi-day alpine objective rather than a day-approach crag. For this specific route: The Monk is a distinct, smaller detached tower/buttress leaning against Cathedral Peak's south/east flank, not part of the main South Face wall. From Cathedral Lakes camp, follow the same talus slope toward Cathedral Pass but hike up into the deep gully separating Cathedral Peak from The Monk, then start on The Monk's own faces (right side of the gully); most Monk routes descend via rappels down the NE gully.

text.overview: A 5-pitch line up the middle of The Monk's South Face from its lowest point, passing left of the prominent mid-face roof.
text.descent: Rappel the northeast gully in three rappels of about 75 feet (roughly 23 m) each; a single 60 m rope doubled is enough for every rappel. Carry slings and rap rings to back up or build the stations. The gully is the standard way off the Monk, and it deposits you on the talus at the foot of the formation, from where a short walk down talus and slabs returns you to camp at Upper Cathedral Lake.

waypoints.directions: The drive is straightforward: from Winthrop, follow the Chewuch River valley north on West Chewuch Road / FR-51, paved the entire way, about 23 miles to the Andrews Creek Trailhead at roughly 3,040 ft. Andrews Creek Trail #504 leaves from the parking area, and a free self-issue wilderness permit is filled out here — you also need a trailhead parking pass displayed on the car. Day one of the standard plan is a 17 to 20 mile hike to Upper Cathedral Lake, so drive in early and expect to be walking for most of the day. This is a two to four day backpack, so pack the car for a trip, not an outing.

waypoints.directions: Follow Andrews Creek Trail #504 up the valley, much of it through an old burn with little shade, about 12 miles to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft. Drop into the meadow at Spanish Creek, cross the creek and join the Boundary Trail, following it east until a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lake, about 18 miles from the car.

The routes start on The Monk's own rock on the right side of the gully, 30 to 40 minutes from camp.

text.overview: A short 1-2 pitch route up the left of a pair of cracks at the lower left side of The Monk's South Face, cruxing in a chimney near the top.
text.descent: Short enough to rappel the route on gear from the top of the second pitch. If you link into the upper formation and top out on The Monk, descend the northeast gully with three 75-foot rappels — a doubled 60 m rope covers each. waypoints.name: Andrews Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: The driving is the easy part of this trip. From Winthrop, head north up the Chewuch River valley on West Chewuch Road / FR-51 — paved the whole way — about 23 miles to the Andrews Creek Trailhead at roughly 3,040 ft, where Andrews Creek Trail #504 starts. Fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead and leave a trailhead parking pass on the car. Everything difficult is on the far side of the parking lot: the walk in runs around 18 miles one way, so load the car for a multi-day trip rather than a day out.

waypoints.name: Upper Cathedral Lake
waypoints.note: The usual base camp for The Monk and Cathedral Peak; the climbing is done from here.
waypoints.directions: Follow Andrews Creek Trail #504 up the valley, much of it through an old burn with little shade, about 12 miles to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft. Drop into the meadow at Spanish Creek, cross the creek and join the Boundary Trail, following it east until a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lake, about 18 miles from the car.

waypoints.name: Base of The Monk
waypoints.note: Left of the two West Cracks lines, on the lower left side of The Monk's south face.
waypoints.directions: From camp, walk up through meadows and talus toward Cathedral Pass, then turn up into the deep gully between Cathedral Peak's south wall and The Monk, the small tower leaning against the wall's lower right side. The routes start on The Monk's own rock on the right side of the gully, 30 to 40 minutes from camp.

waypoints.name: The Monk (tower top)
waypoints.note: The route itself is one or two pitches; carrying on to the top of the tower commits you to the three northeast-gully rappels.

name: The Monk - West Cracks - Right Crack

text.approach: The drive itself is easy — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek Trailhead, about 23 miles total — but the climb to Cathedral Peak is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state. From the trailhead, the Andrews Creek Trail (#504) climbs roughly 12 miles to 6,680+ ft Andrews Pass, then descends into the Spanish Creek drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lakes below the peak's southwest side, putting the one-way approach at around 18 miles with significant elevation gain and loss along the way. Most parties treat this as a 2-4 day backpack (roughly 40+ miles round trip), camping at or near Cathedral Lakes before making a summit push. A free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead, along with a trailhead parking pass; the first many miles are a hot, rocky, buggy uphill slog with little shade, so this is genuinely a remote, multi-day alpine objective rather than a day-approach crag. For this specific route: The Monk is a distinct, smaller detached tower/buttress leaning against Cathedral Peak's south/east flank, not part of the main South Face wall. From Cathedral Lakes camp, follow the same talus slope toward Cathedral Pass but hike up into the deep gully separating Cathedral Peak from The Monk, then start on The Monk's own faces (right side of the gully); most Monk routes descend via rappels down the NE gully.

text.overview: The technical line up Pyramid's east side, climbed as the 5th of 14 summits during the first complete Southern Pickets Enchainment; rated II 5.8, with rock the first party found 'surprisingly beautiful' despite the peak's chossy reputation.

text.approach: Same trailhead and initial approach as the East Peak standard route: Hidden Lake Trailhead via Cascade River Road and FSR 1540, then Hidden Lake Trail #745 to Sibley Pass (~6,040–6,060 ft). From the pass, rather than dropping toward Hidden Lake Basin, follow the ridge crest and the faint climbers' trail east toward West Triad.

text.overview: A long, loose ridge traverse across all three of The Triad's summits (West, Middle, East), with sustained exposed 4th-class and low-5th-class scrambling and a 5.6 R crux pitch on Middle Triad's west face — among the least-documented lines in the Boston Basin/Eldorado group.
text.descent: Parties descending off the Triad ridge toward the Eldorado Glacier have reported pushing past refrigerator- to car-sized loose blocks and down-climbing roughly 500 ft of exposed 5.6–5.7 terrain to reach the glacier — one party called it among the boldest down-climbing they had committed to. name: Middle Peak via South Face - South Chimney

text.approach: Same trailhead and initial trail as the East/Main Peak standard route: Mineral Creek Trailhead (2,400 ft), across the Kachess River ford, 1.7 miles of trail to the Mineral Creek crossing, then about 1 mile through vine maple brush to the base of the south-side talus slope below Middle Peak. As of late May 2026 a gate stands near the old trailhead and the trail now starts from a small lot (4-5 cars) at the end of a narrow logging road; a short descent leads to the first log crossing. The Kachess River and Mineral Creek are both crossed on logs in June and July; the logs are bare and slick, so some parties sit and shuffle across.

text.overview: A distinct line up Three Queens' Middle Peak (6,600 ft), climbing the south face to a rock gable below the summit and finishing up a class 4 chimney system; it has been climbed solo, car-to-car, as a day scramble/climb.
text.descent: From the summit, set up two sequential 60-ft (18m) rappels down the South Chimney to regain the south-facing ledge below the rock gable. From there, downclimb/traverse back toward the Main-Middle notch area and descend the talus slope, retracing the brushy off-trail section and the Mineral Creek trail back to the trailhead and river ford.

waypoints.name: Mineral Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From Cle Elum, drive Highway 903 north about 17 miles, past Lake Cle Elum, and turn left onto Cooper Lake Road (FR 4600). Follow FR 4600 about 7 miles, past the Cooper Lake turnoff, to Cooper Pass. Stay on the main road about 3 miles down to the small signed Mineral Creek trailhead in the valley bottom, at about 2,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

text.approach: From the Mineral Creek Trailhead (2,400 ft), follow the Kachess River/Mineral Creek approach through Park Lakes to Spectacle Point (5,800 ft) — a longer multi-day approach (16 miles round trip in the accounts report) than the Middle Peak day-route.

text.overview: A rock scramble/climb up Three Queens' West Peak (6,400 ft) via its West Ridge and West Face, approached from a high camp at Spectacle Point after a multi-day hike in via Mineral Creek and Park Lakes.
text.descent: Descend the West Ridge/West Face by the ascent line back to Spectacle Point, then follow the Park Lakes-Mineral Creek trail back out to the Mineral Creek Trailhead.

text.approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of Cascade River Road, ~23.1 mi from Marblemount), travel via Cascade Pass or the nearby Alliteration Col and descend/traverse east through the Pelton Basin area to Trapper Lake (el. ~4,170 ft), sitting just northeast of Trapper Mountain. From the lake, boot or skin directly to the base of the obvious north-facing couloir splitting the summit block, switching to crampons/ski (ascent) plates as the snow firms up higher on the route.

text.overview: A prominent north-facing snow/ice couloir splitting Trapper Mountain's summit block above Trapper Lake, climbed on foot and skied/split-boarded as a steep ski-mountaineering descent.
text.descent: The couloir is typically descended on skis/splitboard by the same line, managing sluff in the sustained 45-50 degree middle section; parties have encountered moats and debris (rock, fallen trees, ice chunks) piled at the base near Trapper Lake by early summer. waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.directions: From Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road east about 23.1 miles to where it ends at the Cascade Pass Trailhead, roughly 3,660 feet. Park in the lot at the road end; everything on this route starts there, heading up toward Cascade Pass or the nearby Alliteration Col.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.directions: Follow the Cascade Pass Trail as it switchbacks up through forest and then traverses open slopes to the pass, about 3.7 miles and 1,700 ft above the lot.

waypoints.name: Trapper Lake
waypoints.directions: From the pass descend east into Pelton Basin. Beyond the basin there is no trail: cross Pelton Creek, work southeast up the shoulder of Pelton Peak to the saddle above Trapper Lake, then descend very steeply to the lake at about 4,170 ft. The peak and its north couloir stand directly across the water to the southwest.

waypoints.name: Top of the North Couloir
waypoints.note: The couloir tops out on the crest with a view over the south side. The ground from here to the true summit is not well known; most parties turn around or ski from here.
waypoints.directions: Boot up the debris fan from the lake and get across the moat at the foot of the chute, then climb the couloir: moderate low down, sustained in the 50s through the middle, and firmest and bumpiest in the last 500 ft to the top.

text.approach: Ferry/floatplane to Stehekin (no road access), then the Company Creek Trail roughly 3 miles to a point below Tupshin's west side. Leave the trail and scramble up White Goat Mountain's west slopes through dense brush, traversing rightward through the 4,200-4,600 ft band, then cross a roughly 7,200 ft pass above Bird Lakes and descend into the Bird Lakes basin below Tupshin's east face (face starts ~7,600 ft). Most parties in July to September go in by the Devore Creek trail to the Bird Creek camp near 5,400-5,500 ft, then fight slide alder up to a basin camp around 5,800 ft; easy slopes lead to a ridge near 7,000 ft, then a descending traverse to the snow basin east of the summit block.

text.overview: A longer, harder technical line up Tupshin's east face, reached via a demanding cross-country approach from Company Creek over a pass above Bird Lakes; class 2-4 ledge scrambling leads to a short, poorly-protected 5.4-5.6 crux below the summit.
text.descent: Downclimb the summit pitch and upper class 4 terrain back through the ledge system, taking care around the crux flake/crack; parties have used a 30 m rope for the technical sections. Continue down the zigzagging ledges and the lower class 2-3 ramp back to the basin below the face, then reverse the cross-country traverse over the pass above Bird Lakes to Company Creek Trail.
